vsm1.2:23.1:
ii. Next there is the triple-robe-wearer’s practice. This is undertaken with one of the following
statements: “I refuse a fourth robe”
vsm1.2:23.3:
When a triple-robe wearer has got cloth for a robe, he can put it by for as long
as, owing to ill-health, he is unable to make it up,
vsm1.2:23.4: or for as long as he does not find a helper, or lacks a needle, etc., and there is no fault in his putting it by.
vsm1.2:23.5: But it is not allowed to put it by once it has been dyed.
vsm1.2:23.6: That is called cheating the ascetic practice. These are the directions for it.
vsm1.2:24.2:
Herein, one who is strict should, at the time of dyeing, first dye either the inner cloth or the upper
garment, and having dyed it, he should wear that round the waist and dye the other.
vsm1.2:24.3: Then he can put that on over the shoulder and dye the cloak of patches.
vsm1.2:24.4: But he is not allowed to wear the cloak of patches round the waist. This is the duty when in an abode inside a village.
vsm1.2:24.5: But it is allowable for him in the forest to wash and dye two together.
vsm1.2:24.6: However, he should sit in a place near to the robes so that, if he sees anyone, he can pull a yellow cloth over himself.
vsm1.2:24.7: But for the medium one there is a yellow cloth in the dyeing room for use while dyeing,
vsm1.2:24.8: and it is allowable for him to wear that as an inner cloth or to put it on as an upper garment in order to do the work of dyeing.
vsm1.2:24.9:
For the mild one it is allowable to wear, or put on, the robes of bhikkhus who are in communion (i.e.
not suspended, etc.) in order to do the work of dyeing.
vsm1.2:24.10: A bedspread that remains where it is is also allowable for him, but he must not take it about him.
vsm1.2:24.11: And it is allowed for him to use from time to time the robes of bhikkhus who are in communion.
vsm1.2:24.12: It is allowed to one who wears the triple robe as an ascetic practice to have a yellow shoulder-cloth too as a fourth;
vsm1.2:24.13: but it must be only a span wide and three hands long.
vsm1.2:24.14:
The moment anyone of these three agrees to accept a fourth robe, his ascetic
practice is broken. This is the breach in this instance.
vsm1.2:25.1: The benefits are these. The bhikkhu who is a triple-robe wearer is content with the robe as a protection for the body.
vsm1.2:25.2:
Hence he goes taking it with him as a bird does its wings (M I 180); and such special
qualities as having few undertakings, avoidance of storage of cloth,
vsm1.2:25.3:
a frugal existence, the abandoning of greed for many robes, living in effacement by observing moderation
even in what is permitted, production of the fruits of fewness of wishes, etc., are perfected.
vsm1.2:26.1:
No risk of hoarding haunts the man of wit
Who wants no extra cloth for requisite;
Using the triple robe where’er he goes
The pleasant relish of content he knows.
vsm1.2:26.2:
So, would the adept wander undeterred
With naught else but his robes, as flies the bird
With its own wings, then let him too rejoice
That frugalness in garments be his choice.
vsm1.2:26.3:
This is the commentary on the undertaking, directions, grades,
breach, and benefits, in the case of the triple-robe-wearer’s practice.
vsm1.2:27.1: iii. The alms-food-eater’s practice is undertaken with one of the following statements: “I refuse a supplementary food supply”
vsm1.2:27.3:
Now, this alms-food eater should not accept the following fourteen kinds of meal: a meal offered to the Order,
a meal offered to specified bhikkhus, an invitation, a meal given by a ticket, one each half-moon day,
vsm1.2:27.4: one each Uposatha day, one each first of the half-moon, a meal given for visitors, a meal for travellers, a meal for the sick,
vsm1.2:27.5: a meal for sick-nurses, a meal supplied to a particular residence, a meal given in a principal house, a meal given in turn.
vsm1.2:27.6:
If, instead of saying “Take a meal given to the Order”, meals are given saying “The Order
is taking alms in our house; you may take alms too”,
vsm1.2:27.8:
Tickets from the Order that are not for actual food, and also a meal cooked in a monastery,
are allowable as well. These are the directions for it.
vsm1.2:28.2:
Herein, one who is strict takes alms brought both from before and from behind, and he
gives the bowl to those who take it while he stands outside a door.
vsm1.2:28.3: He also takes alms brought to the refectory and given there.
vsm1.2:28.4: But he does not take alms by sitting and waiting for it to be brought later that day.
vsm1.2:28.5: The medium one takes it as well by sitting and waiting for it to be brought later that day;
vsm1.2:28.6: but he does not consent to its being brought the next day.
vsm1.2:28.7: The mild one consents to alms being brought on the next day and on the day after.
vsm1.2:28.8: Both these last miss the joy of an independent life.
vsm1.2:28.9:
There is, perhaps, a preaching on the Noble Ones’ heritages (A II 28) in some village.
The strict one says to the others “Let us go, friends, and listen to the Dhamma.”
vsm1.2:28.10:
One of them says, “I have been made to sit and wait by a man, venerable sir,” and the other,
“I have consented to receive alms tomorrow, venerable sir.”
vsm1.2:28.11: So they are both losers. The other wanders for alms in the morning and then he goes and savours the taste of the Dhamma.
vsm1.2:28.12:
The moment anyone of these three agrees to the extra gain consisting of a meal
given to the Order, etc., his ascetic practice is broken.
vsm1.2:28.13: This is the breach in this instance.
vsm1.2:29.2:
idleness is eliminated; livelihood is purified; the practice of the minor training
rule of the Pātimokkha is fulfilled; he is not maintained by another;
vsm1.2:29.3:
he helps others; pride is abandoned; craving for tastes is checked; the training precepts about eating as a group,
substituting one meal invitation for another (see Vinaya, Pācittiya 33 and Comy.), and good behaviour, are not contravened;
vsm1.2:29.4: his life conforms to the principles of fewness of wishes; he cultivates the right way; he has compassion for later generations.
vsm1.2:30.1:
The monk content with alms for food
Has independent livelihood,
And greed in him no footing finds;
He is as free as the four winds.
vsm1.2:30.2:
He never need be indolent,
His livelihood is innocent,
So let a wise man not disdain
Alms-gathering for his domain.
vsm1.2:30.4:
“If a bhikkhu can support himself on alms
And live without another’s maintenance,
And pay no heed as well to gain and fame,
The very gods indeed might envy him” (Ud 31).
vsm1.2:30.5: This is the commentary on the undertaking, directions, grades, breach and benefits, in the case of the alms-food-eater’s practice.
vsm1.2:31.1: iv. The house-to-house seeker’s practice is undertaken with one of the following statements “I refuse a greedy alms round”
vsm1.2:31.2: or “I undertake the house-to-house seeker’s practice.”
vsm1.2:31.3: Now, the house-to-house seeker should stop at the village gate and make sure that there is no danger.
vsm1.2:31.4: If there is danger in any street or village, it is allowable to leave it out and wander for alms elsewhere.
vsm1.2:31.5: When there is a house door or a street or a village where he regularly gets nothing at all,
vsm1.2:31.6: he can go past it not counting it as a village.
vsm1.2:31.7: But wherever he gets anything at all it is not allowed subsequently to go past there and leave it out.
vsm1.2:31.8: This bhikkhu should enter the village early so that he will be able to leave out any inconvenient place and go elsewhere.
vsm1.2:31.9:
But if people who are giving a gift of a meal in a monastery or who are coming along
the road take his bowl and give alms food, it is allowable.
vsm1.2:31.10:
And as this bhikkhu is going along the road, he should, when it is the time,
wander for alms in any village he comes to and not pass it by.
vsm1.2:31.11: If he gets nothing there or only a little, he should wander for alms in the next village in order. These are the directions for it.
vsm1.2:32.2: Herein, one who is strict does not take alms brought from before or brought from behind or brought to the refectory and given there.
vsm1.2:32.3: He hands over his bowl at a door, however;
vsm1.2:32.4: for in this ascetic practice there is none equal to the Elder Mahā Kassapa,
vsm1.2:32.5: yet an instance in which even he handed over his bowl is mentioned (see Ud 29).
vsm1.2:32.6:
The medium one takes what is brought from before and from behind and what
is brought to the refectory, and he hands over his bowl at a door.
vsm1.2:32.7: But he does not sit waiting for alms. Thus he conforms to the rule of the strict alms-food eater.
vsm1.2:32.8: The mild one sits waiting for alms to be brought that day.
vsm1.2:32.9:
The ascetic practice of these three is broken as soon as the greedy alms round starts by going
only to the houses where good alms food is given. This is the breach in this instance.
vsm1.2:33.1: The benefits are these. He is always a stranger among families and is like the moon (S II 197); he abandons avarice about families;
vsm1.2:33.2:
he is compassionate impartially; he avoids the dangers in being supported by a family; he does not delight in invitations;
he does not hope for meals to be brought; his life conforms to the principles of fewness of wishes, and so on.
vsm1.2:34.1:
The monk who at each house his begging plies
Is moonlike, ever new to families,
Nor does he grudge to help all equally,
Free from the risks of house-dependency.
vsm1.2:34.2:
Who would the self-indulgent round forsake
And roam the world at will, the while to make
His downcast eyes range a yoke-length before,
Then let him wisely seek from door to door.
vsm1.2:34.3:
This is the commentary on the undertaking, directions, grades,
breach, and benefits, in the case of the house-to-house-seeker’s practice.
